summary: Hebrew numbers have gender. From 1 to 19 every number has a masculine and a feminine form, chosen by the gender of the noun you count: שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים “three books” (סֵפֶר is masculine), שָׁלוֹשׁ מִטּוֹת “three beds” (מִטָּה is feminine). Surprisingly, for 3–10 the form with the ending -ָה, which looks feminine, goes with masculine nouns — an old Semitic pattern that Arabic shares. When you simply count (and in phone numbers, prices and sums) you use the feminine: אַחַת, שְׁתַּיִם, שָׁלוֹשׁ, אַרְבַּע … The number stands before the noun, except אֶחָד / אַחַת, which follows it like an adjective (סֵפֶר אֶחָד). Two has a short (construct) form before nouns: שְׁנֵי סְפָרִים, שְׁתֵּי מִטּוֹת. Before a definite masculine noun, 3–10 take a construct form in -ֶת: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַסְּפָרִים “the three books”. The tens (עֶשְׂרִים, שְׁלוֹשִׁים …) never change, and 21 is said ten first: עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת. מֵאָה “100” and אֶלֶף “1000” have a dual for 200 and 2000 (מָאתַיִם, אַלְפַּיִם): the dual ending -ַיִם is still alive for “two” of a few things (יוֹמַיִם “two days”). From 2 on, the counted noun is plural.

blocks.title: Ask the noun, not the number
blocks.text: First find the gender of the noun — from its singular. חַלּוֹן is masculine, so שְׁלוֹשָׁה חַלּוֹנוֹת, although the plural ends in -וֹת; נָשִׁים is feminine, so שָׁלוֹשׁ נָשִׁים.

blocks.title: The ending -ָה lies
blocks.text: From 3 to 10 the form in -ָה goes with masculine nouns: שְׁלוֹשָׁה יְלָדִים “three boys”, but שָׁלוֹשׁ יְלָדוֹת “three girls”. Arabic does exactly the same: ثَلَاثَةُ أَوْلَادٍ, ثَلَاثُ بَنَاتٍ.

blocks.title: One after, two shortened, “the” in -ֶת
blocks.text: סֵפֶר אֶחָד, מִטָּה אַחַת — one follows the noun. Two before a noun is always שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי. Before a definite masculine noun 3–10 end in -ֶת / -ַת: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַיְּלָדִים, עֲשֶׂרֶת הַתַּלְמִידִים.

blocks.title: Counting, prices, phone numbers
blocks.text: Israelis count in the feminine: אַחַת, שְׁתַּיִם, שָׁלוֹשׁ … In casual speech you will also hear feminine numbers with masculine nouns; the standard — and what this course teaches — is to match the noun: שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים.

blocks.title: The dual is alive
blocks.text: A few words keep the old dual ending -ַיִם for exactly two: יוֹמַיִם “two days”, שְׁבוּעַיִם “two weeks”, שְׁנָתַיִם “two years”, פַּעֲמַיִם “twice”, מָאתַיִם “200”, אַלְפַּיִם “2000”. Paired body parts use it as their plural: עֵינַיִם “eyes”, יָדַיִם “hands”, רַגְלַיִם “legs”.

blocks.title: Age is feminine
blocks.text: Age in years is said with בֶּן / בַּת and the feminine number, because שָׁנִים “years” is feminine: הוּא בֶּן שָׁלוֹשׁ, הִיא בַּת עֶשְׂרִים.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you say a number
questions: What is the gender of the noun (look at the singular)?
Is it one (after the noun) or two (שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי)?
Is the noun definite — then the construct form?
Am I just counting — then the feminine?

askYourself: What is the gender of the noun I count — from its singular (חַלּוֹן m., כּוֹס f.)?
Is it one? → אֶחָד / אַחַת after the noun.
Is it two? → שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי before the noun (שְׁנַיִם / שְׁתַּיִם only alone).
3–10 with a masculine noun? → the form in -ָה; with a feminine noun → the short form.
Is the noun definite (“the three …”)? → masculine 3–10 take the construct: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַ…
Am I just counting, or saying a phone number or a price? → the feminine form.
From two on: is my noun in the plural?
steps: Find the noun and its gender.
Pick the masculine or feminine number.
Use the construct form before a definite noun (and always for 2).
Put one after the noun, every other number before it.

traps: *שָׁלוֹשׁ סְפָרִים — סֵפֶר is masculine: שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים.
חַלּוֹנוֹת looks feminine but is masculine: שְׁלוֹשָׁה חַלּוֹנוֹת, not *שָׁלוֹשׁ חַלּוֹנוֹת.
*אֶחָד סֵפֶר — one comes after the noun: סֵפֶר אֶחָד.
*שְׁנַיִם סְפָרִים — before a noun: שְׁנֵי סְפָרִים.
*שְׁלוֹשָׁה הַסְּפָרִים — before a definite noun: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַסְּפָרִים.
*עֶשְׂרִים סֵפֶר — after a number the noun is plural: עֶשְׂרִים סְפָרִים (a few nouns such as שָׁנָה may stay singular after big numbers: עֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה).
In 21–99 the unit follows the ten with וְ and still agrees with the noun: עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים, עֶשְׂרִים וְשָׁלוֹשׁ מִטּוֹת (וְ becomes וּ before a shva).
Age in years is feminine, because שָׁנִים is feminine: הוּא בֶּן שָׁלוֹשׁ “he is three” — but בֶּן שְׁלוֹשָׁה חֳדָשִׁים “three months old” (חֹדֶשׁ is masculine).

quiz.why: A masculine noun takes the form in -ָה (3–10); the construct שְׁלוֹשֶׁת is only for a definite noun (שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַסְּפָרִים).
One follows the noun and agrees with it: מִטָּה is feminine, so אַחַת.
Before a noun two is always the construct form, and כּוֹס is feminine: שְׁתֵּי. שְׁתַּיִם stands alone.
Before a definite masculine noun 3–10 take the construct form in -ֶת: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַ…
Counting uses the feminine forms, and the absolute שְׁתַּיִם (שְׁתֵּי needs a noun after it).
חַלּוֹן is masculine — the plural ending -וֹת does not change that — so the masculine שִׁבְעָה.
Two hundred is the dual of מֵאָה: מָאתַיִם (as 2000 is אַלְפַּיִם).

seeAlso.note: Arabic has the same reversed gender for 3–10 (ثَلَاثَةُ أَوْلَادٍ, ثَلَاثُ بَنَاتٍ) and a living dual; after 11–99 the Arabic noun is singular, the Hebrew one plural.
German has one form for each number (only ein / eine agrees) and puts the unit first (einundzwanzig); Hebrew says עֶשְׂרִים וְאֶחָד, like English twenty-one.
Chinese needs a measure word between the number and the noun (三本书) and has two words for two (二 / 两); the noun never changes.
